## The Estimator

When the treatment is endogenous we can still identify **quantile treatment effects for compliers**
— the subpopulation whose treatment status responds to the instrument. Under the LATE assumptions
(independence, exclusion, monotonicity and a relevant first stage), Abadie's kappa weighting
identifies the complier potential-outcome distribution ([Abadie 2003](#ref-abadie-2003);
[Frölich & Melly 2013](#ref-frolich-melly-2013)):

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{Y(d)\mid c}(y) &= \frac{E\!\left[w_d\,\mathbb{1}\{Y \le y\}\right]}{E[w_d]}, \\[2pt]
w_1 &= \frac{D\,\bigl(Z - \pi(X)\bigr)}{\pi(X)\,\bigl(1 - \pi(X)\bigr)}, \\[2pt]
w_0 &= \frac{(1 - D)\,\bigl(\pi(X) - Z\bigr)}{\pi(X)\,\bigl(1 - \pi(X)\bigr)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $\pi(X) = P(Z = 1 \mid X)$ is the instrument probability, estimated by a logit. The local
quantile treatment effect is the difference between the two complier quantiles,
$\Delta_\tau = Q_\tau(Y(1)\mid c) - Q_\tau(Y(0)\mid c)$, and the average effect is the LATE.
`estimate_unconditional_local_effects` inverts the signed weighted empirical CDFs to obtain the
quantile effects and reports bootstrap standard errors.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| code-summary: "Show code (setup, side-by-side, timing and descriptive-stats helpers)"
import time

import polars as pl
import vl_convert as vlc
from great_tables import GT
from IPython.display import HTML

from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig
from qte.constants import _make_q
from qte.datasets import load_card, load_jtpa
from qte.iv import estimate_unconditional_local_effects

QS = _make_q(20)  # 0.05, 0.10, ..., 0.95
REPORT = [0.10, 0.50, 0.90]
BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=3, seed=42, n_workers=4)


def side_by_side(result, report: list[float] | None = None) -> HTML:
    """Render a result's QTE plot and summary table side by side.

    The plot shows every estimated quantile; the table reports only ``report``.
    """
    svg = vlc.vegalite_to_svg(result.plot().to_dict())
    table = result.tabulate(quantiles=report).as_raw_html()
    return HTML('<div class="iv-side">' f"<div>{svg}</div><div>{table}</div></div>")


class timer:
    """Report how long a block took, like the knitr ``time_it`` hook."""

    def __init__(self, label: str) -> None:
        self.label = label

    def __enter__(self) -> "timer":
        self._start = time.perf_counter()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc: object) -> None:
        print(f"[{self.label}] {time.perf_counter() - self._start:.2f}s")


def descriptive_statistics(
    ds: pl.DataFrame,
    instrument: str,
    variables: list[str],
    labels: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    title: str = "Descriptive statistics by instrument value",
) -> GT:
    """Means of ``variables`` for all units and by instrument arm."""
    labels = labels or {}
    z1 = pl.col(instrument) == 1
    stats = pl.DataFrame(
        [
            {
                "Variable": labels.get(v, v),
                "All": ds[v].mean(),
                "Z = 1": ds.filter(z1)[v].mean(),
                "Z = 0": ds.filter(~z1)[v].mean(),
            }
            for v in variables
        ]
    )
    observations = pl.DataFrame(
        {
            "Variable": ["Observations"],
            "All": [float(ds.height)],
            "Z = 1": [float(ds.filter(z1).height)],
            "Z = 0": [float(ds.filter(~z1).height)],
        }
    )
    stats = pl.concat([observations, stats], how="vertical")
    value_columns = ["All", "Z = 1", "Z = 0"]
    return (
        GT(stats)
        .cols_label(Variable="")
        .fmt_number(columns=value_columns, decimals=2, use_seps=True)
        .fmt_number(columns=value_columns, rows=0, decimals=0, use_seps=True)
        .tab_header(title=title)
    )
```

## Returns to College ([Card, 1995](#ref-card-1995))

The `card` data record log wages (`lwage`), completed college (`college`) and whether the man grew
up near a four-year college (`nearc4`). We use college proximity as an instrument for college
completion. The first stage is modest (about 7 percentage points), so we take the instrument
probability to be constant rather than modelling it on covariates.

```{python}
#| label: card-data
#| code-summary: "Show code (Card descriptive statistics)"
card = load_card()
descriptive_statistics(
    card,
    "nearc4",
    ["lwage", "college", "exper", "educ", "age", "black", "smsa", "south"],
    labels={
        "lwage": "Log wage",
        "college": "College",
        "exper": "Experience",
        "educ": "Years of education",
        "age": "Age",
        "black": "Black",
        "smsa": "SMSA",
        "south": "South",
    },
    title="Table 1. Card data, by college proximity",
)
```

```{python}
#| label: card-estimate
#| code-summary: "Show code (local QTE on the Card data)"
with timer("card"):
    card_res = estimate_unconditional_local_effects(
        card,
        "lwage",
        "college",
        "nearc4",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: card-plot
#| code-summary: "Show code (Card QTE plot)"
print(f"First stage (= complier share) = {card_res.first_stage:.3f}")
side_by_side(card_res, REPORT)
```

The estimated quantile effects rise with the quantile, and the average effect (red) is positive and
significant. As usual for a quantile approach, the picture is richer than the single LATE: the
return to college is much larger at the top of the wage distribution than in the left tail.

## Training and Earnings (JTPA)

The `jtpa` data come from the Job Training Partnership Act study, which randomly assigned applicants
to a treatment group eligible for training. Because only about two thirds of those assigned actually
enrol, assignment (`assignmt`) is a valid instrument for training (`training`). We use the subsample
of women, following [Abadie, Angrist & Imbens (2002)](#ref-aai-2002).

```{python}
#| label: jtpa-data
#| code-summary: "Show code (JTPA descriptive statistics)"
jtpa = load_jtpa().filter(pl.col("sex") == 0)
descriptive_statistics(
    jtpa,
    "assignmt",
    ["earnings", "training", "age", "black", "hispanic", "married", "hsorged", "afdc", "prevearn"],
    labels={
        "earnings": "Earnings",
        "training": "Training",
        "age": "Age",
        "black": "Black",
        "hispanic": "Hispanic",
        "married": "Married",
        "hsorged": "HS or GED",
        "afdc": "AFDC",
        "prevearn": "Prior earnings",
    },
    title="Table 2. JTPA women, by assignment",
)
```

```{python}
#| label: jtpa-estimate
#| code-summary: "Show code (local QTE on the JTPA data)"
jtpa_covariates = (
    "black + hispanic + married + hsorged + afdc + f2sms + wkless13 "
    "+ age2225 + age2629 + age3035 + age3644 + age4554 + class_tr + ojt_jsa + prevearn"
)
with timer("jtpa"):
    jtpa_res = estimate_unconditional_local_effects(
        jtpa,
        "earnings",
        "training",
        "assignmt",
        qs=QS,
        instrument_probability_formula=jtpa_covariates,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: jtpa-plot
#| code-summary: "Show code (JTPA QTE plot)"
print(f"First stage (= complier share) = {jtpa_res.first_stage:.3f}")
side_by_side(jtpa_res, REPORT)
```

For women the training effect is positive at every quantile and largest around the median. The
average effect (red) is positive and clearly different from zero, matching the distributional
pattern emphasised by [Abadie, Angrist & Imbens (2002)](#ref-aai-2002).

## Simulated Data

The two applications above use real data, so the truth is unknown. To check that the estimator
recovers the target when its assumptions hold, we simulate data where the complier quantile effects
are known. The design follows the JTPA-based simulation of
[Kaplan & Sun (2017)](#ref-kaplan-sun-2017).

Each observation is characterized by a single (observed) covariate and a latent (unobserved) type
$u_i$. They are generated via:

$$
x_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \qquad u_i \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1],
$$

The instrument's value, $Z_i$, is random and whether the instrument is switched on depends on
covariates. The strength of that dependence is controlled by the `instrument_propensity_slope`. The
baseline propensity to be assigned is $p_0$ (the `offer_probability` parameter).

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_i = P(Z_i = 1 \mid x_i) &= \sigma\!\left(\operatorname{logit}(p_0) + \texttt{instrument\_propensity\_slope} \cdot x_i\right), \\
Z_i &\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i),
\end{aligned}
$$

The treatment's potential values are determined as follows: first, there is one-sided non-compliance
in the sense that if the instrument is switched off the unit will never get treated (there are no
always-takers). Compliance with the treatment if the instrument is switched on is random. First
there is a take-up threshold $T(x_i)$ that determines beyond which type, as measured by $u_i$,
treatment is certain with the instrument switched on. For $u_i$ realizations below the threshold,
take-up is probabilistic for the case of a switched-on instrument. The threshold $T(x_i)$ itself
depends on a base threshold that determines the take-up threshold at $x_i = 0$, which is here the
mean of the covariate. As $x_i$ increases the take-up threshold increases as well.

$$
\begin{aligned}
T(x_i) &= \texttt{base\_takeup\_threshold} \cdot \exp\!\left(\texttt{takeup\_threshold\_slope} \cdot x_i\right), \\
D_i(1) &\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}\!\left(\min\{1, u_i / T(x_i)\}\right), \qquad D_i(0) = 0, \\
D_i &= Z_i \cdot D_i(1),
\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, potential outcomes under no treatment are determined by covariates and the type, where a
larger type at equal covariates means a higher outcome under no treatment. Lastly, the potential
outcome under treatment is given by the outcome under no treatment plus a scaled version of the
type.

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_i(0) &= \texttt{covariate\_effect} \cdot x_i + \Phi^{-1}(u_i), \\
Y_i(1) &= Y_i(0) + \texttt{effect\_scale} \cdot u_i, \\
Y_i &= D_i \cdot Y_i(1) + (1 - D_i) \cdot Y_i(0),
\end{aligned}
$$

Economically, in this model compliers tend to have a higher $U_i$ and also a higher benefit from the
treatment. This means the LATE is pushed above the ATE. Lastly, the AAI-style weight
$\nu_0(U) = E[Z \mid U] = P(Z = 1 \mid Y, D, X)$, with $U = (Y, D, X)$, is explicit here since
$D = 1 \implies Z = 1$:

$$
\nu_0(U) = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } D = 1, \\
\dfrac{p\,(1 - q)}{1 - p\,q} & \text{if } D = 0,
\end{cases}
$$

where $p = P(Z = 1 \mid X)$, $q = \min\{1, u / T(X)\}$, and
$u = \Phi(Y - \texttt{covariate\_effect} \cdot X)$ on the $D = 0$ branch.

### Unconditional LATE without Covariates

We start with a scenario where covariates do not matter for the instrument assignment probability
and for the selection into treatment. The latter, thus, only depends on the latent type.

```{python}
#| label: simulation
#| code-summary: "Show code (simulate the data and recover the true LATE)"
from qte.iv.simulate import get_true_local_effects, simulate_data

simulated_data = simulate_data(n=100_000, seed=0)
truth, late = get_true_local_effects(QS, n_oracle=1_000_000, seed=0)
print(f"True LATE = {late:.3f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: simulation-estimate
#| code-summary: "Show code (estimate the local QTE)"
with timer("simulation"):
    sim_res = estimate_unconditional_local_effects(
        simulated_data, "y", "treatment", "instrument", qs=QS, bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: simulation-comparison
#| code-summary: "Show code (IV vs. naive comparisons)"


def naive_quantile_effect(ds: pl.DataFrame, group: str) -> pl.Series:
    """Quantile difference between the two values of ``group``, ignoring endogeneity."""
    one = ds.filter(pl.col(group) == 1)["y"]
    zero = ds.filter(pl.col(group) == 0)["y"]
    return pl.Series([one.quantile(q) - zero.quantile(q) for q in QS], dtype=pl.Float64)


comparison = (
    sim_res.qtt.select(pl.col("q"), pl.col("effect").alias("IV"), pl.col("se"))
    .with_columns(truth["effect"].alias("Truth"))
    .with_columns(naive_quantile_effect(simulated_data, "treatment").alias("Naive (D)"))
    .with_columns(naive_quantile_effect(simulated_data, "instrument").alias("ITT (Z)"))
    .filter(pl.col("q").is_in(REPORT))
)
(
    GT(comparison)
    .fmt_number(["IV", "Truth", "Naive (D)", "ITT (Z)", "se"], decimals=3)
    .tab_header(title="Table 3. Simulated local QTE, IV vs. naive comparisons")
)
```

```{python}
#| label: simulation-plot
#| code-summary: "Show code (simulated QTE plot)"
print(f"First stage (= complier share) = {sim_res.first_stage:.3f}")
side_by_side(sim_res, REPORT)
```

The IV estimates track the true complier quantile effects closely. The naive comparison by observed
treatment status is far too large because it ignores the endogeneity of take-up, and the
intention-to-treat difference is attenuated by the roughly 62% compliance rate.

Point estimates are only half the story: the reported standard errors should also be well
calibrated. We repeat the estimation on many independent samples and record how often the 95%
bootstrap interval contains the truth, alongside the average standard error and the empirical
standard deviation of the estimates.

```{python}
#| label: simulation-coverage
#| code-summary: "Show code (bootstrap coverage settings)"
import numpy as np

COVERAGE_REPLICATIONS = 5
COVERAGE_SAMPLE_SIZE = 2_000
COVERAGE_BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=3, seed=0, n_workers=4)
COVERAGE_QUANTILES = [0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90]

true_effect = truth["effect"].to_numpy()
covered = np.zeros((COVERAGE_REPLICATIONS, QS.size))
standard_errors = np.zeros((COVERAGE_REPLICATIONS, QS.size))
estimates = np.zeros((COVERAGE_REPLICATIONS, QS.size))
```

```{python}
#| label: simulation-coverage-estimate
#| code-summary: "Show code (coverage over repeated samples)"
with timer("coverage"):
    for replication in range(COVERAGE_REPLICATIONS):
        sample = simulate_data(n=COVERAGE_SAMPLE_SIZE, seed=250_000 + replication)
        res = estimate_unconditional_local_effects(
            sample,
            "y",
            "treatment",
            "instrument",
            qs=QS,
            bootstrap_config=COVERAGE_BOOTSTRAP,
        )
        effect = res.qtt["effect"].to_numpy()
        se = res.qtt["se"].to_numpy()
        estimates[replication] = effect
        standard_errors[replication] = se
        covered[replication] = np.abs(effect - true_effect) <= 1.96 * se
```

```{python}
#| label: simulation-coverage-comparison
#| code-summary: "Show code (coverage table)"
coverage_table = (
    pl.DataFrame(
        {
            "q": QS,
            "Coverage": covered.mean(axis=0),
            "Mean SE": standard_errors.mean(axis=0),
            "Empirical SD": estimates.std(axis=0),
        }
    )
    .filter(pl.col("q").is_in(COVERAGE_QUANTILES))
)
(
    GT(coverage_table)
    .fmt_number(["Coverage"], decimals=3)
    .fmt_number(["Mean SE", "Empirical SD"], decimals=3)
    .tab_header(title="Table 4. Coverage of the 95% bootstrap interval")
)
```

At every reported quantile the coverage is close to the nominal 0.95, and the mean standard error
tracks the empirical standard deviation of the estimates. The bootstrap intervals can therefore be
trusted in this design, not just the point estimates.

## Unconditional LATE with Covariate Dependent Instrument Slope

Now the instrument probability does depend on the value of the covariate.

```{python}
#| label: simulation-covariates
#| code-summary: "Show code (simulate data with a covariate-dependent instrument probability)"
COVARIATE = {"instrument_propensity_slope": 1.0}

cov = simulate_data(n=100_000, seed=0, **COVARIATE)
cov_truth, _ = get_true_local_effects(QS, n_oracle=1_000_000, seed=0, **COVARIATE)
```

```{python}
#| label: simulation-covariates-estimate
#| code-summary: "Show code (estimate the local QTE with and without the covariate)"
COVARIATE_BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=3, seed=0, n_workers=4)
with timer("covariates"):
    constant_res = estimate_unconditional_local_effects(
        cov, "y", "treatment", "instrument", qs=QS, bootstrap_config=COVARIATE_BOOTSTRAP
    )
    adjusted_res = estimate_unconditional_local_effects(
        cov,
        "y",
        "treatment",
        "instrument",
        qs=QS,
        instrument_probability_formula="x",
        bootstrap_config=COVARIATE_BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: simulation-covariates-comparison
#| code-summary: "Show code (true effect vs. constant and adjusted propensity)"
covariate_table = (
    cov_truth.select(pl.col("q"), pl.col("effect").alias("Truth"))
    .with_columns(constant_res.qtt["effect"].alias("Constant p"))
    .with_columns(adjusted_res.qtt["effect"].alias("Adjusted for x"))
    .filter(pl.col("q").is_in(REPORT))
)
(
    GT(covariate_table)
    .fmt_number(["Truth", "Constant p", "Adjusted for x"], decimals=3)
    .tab_header(title="Table 5. Effects with a covariate-dependent instrument probability")
)
```

```{python}
#| label: simulation-covariates-plot
#| code-summary: "Show code (covariate-dependent instrument plot)"
print(f"Adjusted first stage = {adjusted_res.first_stage:.3f}")
side_by_side(adjusted_res, REPORT)
```

Taking the instrument probability to be constant leaves the estimates far too large at every
quantile, while conditioning on `x` tracks the truth. The propensity model is therefore not optional
when the instrument depends on the covariates.

## The Conditional Estimator

`estimate_conditional_local_effects` targets the complier QTE **conditional on the covariates**,
`Q_tau(Y(1) | X, c) - Q_tau(Y(0) | X, c)` ([Abadie, Angrist & Imbens 2002](#ref-aai-2002)); the
estimator used above targets the _marginal_ complier QTE. The two differ whenever the covariates
shift the outcome, because quantiles do not commute with integrating `X` out:

$$
Q_\tau(Y(d) \mid c) \;\neq\; E_X\!\left[Q_\tau(Y(d) \mid X, c)\right],
\qquad
Q_\tau\!\left(c\,x + h(u)\right) \;\neq\; c\,E[x] + Q_\tau\!\left(h(u)\right).
$$

`get_true_conditional_effects` nets the covariate shift `c x` out of the potential outcomes in the
oracle, so the conditional estimator can be checked against _its own_ target rather than the
marginal one.

The estimator follows the plug-in route of [Abadie, Angrist & Imbens (2002)](#ref-aai-2002): it
estimates `nu = E[Z | Y, D, X]` by a series and plugs it into the kappa identity. **The series has
to be flexible in the right direction.** Here `nu` turns out to be a function of `Y - c x`, so a
basis in `Y` alone (which ignores `x`), or even `poly(y, k) + poly(x, k)` (no interactions, hence no
`x^2`, `x^2 y`, ...), cannot represent it. The mis-specified fit produces implied weights
`W+ = E[kappa | Y, D, X]` that dip below zero - whereas the population weights are non-negative -
and the weighted quantile regression then minimises a non-convex objective and is biased. A generic
two-dimensional polynomial spans the needed terms, keeps `W+` non-negative, and recovers the
conditional truth.

```{python}
#| label: simulation-conditional
#| code-summary: "Show code (simulate the data and recover the conditional truth)"
from qte.iv.simulate import get_true_conditional_effects

conditional_truth = get_true_conditional_effects(QS, n_oracle=1_000_000, seed=0)
conditional_sim = simulate_data(n=100_000, seed=0)
```

```{python}
#| label: simulation-conditional-estimate
#| code-summary: "Show code (conditional estimator on the simulated data)"
from qte.iv import WeightAdjustment, estimate_conditional_local_effects

with timer("conditional"):
    conditional_res = estimate_conditional_local_effects(
        conditional_sim,
        "y",
        "treatment",
        "instrument",
        qs=QS,
        covariates="x",
        instrument_probability_formula=None,
        weight_formula="poly(y, 6) * poly(x, 6)",
        weight_adjustment=WeightAdjustment.PLUGIN,
        bootstrap_config=BootstrapConfig(n_iter=3, seed=0, n_workers=4),
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: simulation-conditional-comparison
#| code-summary: "Show code (conditional vs. marginal truth)"
conditional_table = (
    conditional_truth.select(pl.col("q"), pl.col("effect").alias("Truth (conditional)"))
    .with_columns(conditional_res.qtt["effect"].alias("Conditional IV"))
    .join(truth.select(pl.col("q"), pl.col("effect").alias("Truth (marginal)")), on="q")
    .filter(pl.col("q").is_in(REPORT))
)
(
    GT(conditional_table)
    .fmt_number(["Truth (conditional)", "Conditional IV", "Truth (marginal)"], decimals=3)
    .tab_header(title="Table 6. Conditional estimator on the simulated data")
)
```

The conditional estimates track the conditional truth (within about `0.05` here) and sit well apart
from the marginal truth in the tails - the same data, answering a different question. The two truth
columns are not interchangeable: a marginal counterfactual quantile cannot be built by averaging
conditional ones, which is exactly why `estimate_unconditional_local_effects` integrates `X` out
before inverting the CDF.

   [doi:10.1111/1468-0262.00270](https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0262.00270)

   [doi:10.1080/07350015.2013.803869](https://doi.org/10.1080/07350015.2013.803869)
5. <a id="ref-kaplan-sun-2017"></a>Kaplan, D. M., & Sun, Y. (2017). Smoothed estimating equations
